Tree Nazis vs Fynbos Taliban

By: Hamilton Wende | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
we look at trees, fynbos and climate change in the Cape

Unique Selling Point:
Great visuals illustrate a hotly debated issue over growing exotic trees or cutting them down to preserve the natural fynbos

Summary:
As climate change ravages the world, South Africa suffers too. One of our most critical problems is the decreasing availability of water across our country. In 2017 Cape Town became the first major world city to come to the brink of a water catastrophe – it was days away from completely running out of water.
There are a number of reasons this happened, but many experts say that the widespread existence of trees not indigenous to South Africa are one of the major reasons that the water table is being lowered, and that precious water needed by people, crops, and the unique fynbos biome are all being threatened by the existence of these trees. They contend that all non-indigenous trees should be removed in order to save our water resources.
And then there are those so-called “Tree Nazis” who say that trees are an essential resource to maintain a proper ecological balance in the area. They say that, of course, planting indigenous trees is to be “lauded”, but that many of what they call the “fynbos Taliban” are being too ideologically purist. They say that many of the foreign trees are healthy for the environment and that, technically, many South African trees would never have been in the Cape anyway, and that it makes sense to cultivate trees that actually grow in the Cape – wherever they come from. They talk of trees “introduced” into the environment rather than being “invasive.”


Further information:
We visit the ARDERNE GARDENS in the suburbs of Cape Town. A beautiful botanical garden and arboretum, it is one of the oldest in South Africa and its chairman, FRANCOIS KRIGE, tells us that not only is it a lovely park that serves the citizens of Cape Town, but that its collection of rare and global plants and trees are an important indicator of the effect that climate change is having on the local environment. What happens to the plants in this garden has important clues as to what is changing in our climate. FRANCOIS owns an indigenous forest near Gansbaai, but he tells us why these other trees and plants also matter.
We also meet LEON VISSER, a passionate arborist and tree climber. There is a more than 100 year old Norfolk pine in the garden. Its growth has not been measured for a number of years. We film LEON climbing the tree with all his ropes, pulleys and equipment and correspondent MACFARLANE MOLELI climbs at least some of the way with him (If he is willing!) It is a fascinating sequence and there is a personal story here too in that LEON lost four fingers in an accident some years ago but it hasn’t stopped him climbing. He feels blessed to be able to do so.
But climbing trees, especially “champion” trees like this Norfolk pine, is more than a hobby for LEON. He tells us – perhaps halfway up the tree, and assisted by drone shots – that what he learns from the growth or lack of it, in this tree is essential to helping us understand the effect that the drought of 2017 had on this ancient tree and, more broadly, what it might mean for climate change in the region.
MACFARLANE then finds himself in a helicopter over the mountains surrounding Cape Town. A team from THE NATURE CONSERVANCY (TNC) part of the The Greater Cape Town Water Fund initiative. Their mission is to monitor water levels in the environment around Cape Town and also to remove invasive vegetation – especially pines and eucalypts.
Today the team, LOUISE STAFFORD, RICHARD BUGAN AND PHILISIWE SHANGE are flying to a remote area in the hills near FRANSHHOEK?? (or wherever). They are checking on their sophisticated scientific equipment that monitors water levels and RICHARD BUGAN, tells us what is finding and why it matters. He and LOUISE tell us that, in fact, these invasive trees are threatening Cape Town’s water supply and the city faces a real threat, sooner rather than later, of hitting “Day Zero” for water.
We film an exciting montage of tree felling while PHILISIWE tells us more about the water situation and why these trees, particularly, pines, have to go. We come away with solid evidence as to why they see non-indigenous trees as a threat to the Cape and South African environment.
[There is a bit of redundancy in having three people interviewed but they want this team to be present so we’ll work it out on the ground and in the edit]
We also film with ANTON MARAIS a beekeeper in Franschhoek. He shows us his hives and his honey bees filling their combs and tells us how important particularly well-established, flowering eucalypts are for agriculture and plant life in general in the Cape.
Finally, we visit MOUNTAIN ROAD PRIMARY in Woodstock where ZOE GAULD ANGELUCCI of the NGO Greenpops shows us the trees they have planted and the indigenous garden that they have begun with the children – “after the drought of 2017, we realized that planting trees wasn’t enough. We needed a more holistic approach. Trees are important but in the current situation we needed to plant a fynbos garden as well.”
The film ends with a montage of children planting fynbos, pouring water – with the trees that have been planted in the background.
Things must change and nurturing the environment demands a balanced approach trees and fynbos can live together, creating a better future for these children…

Script:


TREES AND FYNBOS SCRIPT

THESE BEAUTIFUL MOUNTAINS HOLD CAPE TOWN'S MOST PRECIOUS TREASURE – WATER.

IN 2018, CAPE TOWN NEARLY RAN OUT OF WATER
EXOTIC TREES LIKE PINES AND EUCALYPTS ARE A MAJOR PART OF THE PROBLEM, SUCKING UP WATER FROM THE SOIL.
IT IS NOW ALMOST AN UNQUESTIONED BELIEF THAT NON-INDIGENOUS TREES SHOULD BE ERADICATED. THAT THEY ARE A SERIOUS THREAT TO THE WATER SUPPLY - THAT THEY WERE WRONGLY INTRODUCED DECADES AGO IN THE COLONIAL ERA, TO GRATIFY THE EUROCENTRIC TASTES OF PRIVILIGED WHITES
BUT THERE ARE THOSE WHO SAY THIS IS WRONG, EVEN IRRATIONAL, AND THERE IS MUCH MORE TO CONSIDER. THAT THESE TREES ARE AN INTEGRAL PART OF OUR LIVES AND OF THE WEALTH OF THIS COUNTRY. WE SIMPLY CANNOT DO WITHOUT THEM.
Mac (off camera) “How we getting up here?”
Leon: “So we’re going to climb this tree. We’re not using ladders. We’re going to be using ropes.”
TO SEE WHAT THEY MEAN, WE JOINED ARBORISTS LEON VISSER & FRANCOIS KRIGE IN CAPE TOWN’S HISTORIC ARDERNE GARDENS.
THEY WORK TO PRESERVE LARGE TREES AROUND THE CAPE TOWN AREA IN GARDENS AND PUBLIC SPACES

LEON SAYS THAT EXOTIC TREES HAVE A SIGNIFICANT PLACE IN THE ECOSYSTEM, ESPECIALLY IN CITIES. THEIR EXISTENCE BRINGS VALUE OF THEIR OWN, AESTHETIC AND CULTURAL, THAT PEOPLE NEED DEEPLY
AND THE TREES DESERVE TO BE CARED FOR…
THEY WERE MEASURING ONE OF THE GARDENS’ CHAMPION TREES, A NORFOLK PINE - TO ADD TO THEIR RECORDS OF WHAT TREES EXIST IN THE CITY AS A RESOURCE FOR PEOPLE TO ENJOY


MAC: “I feel like Carteblanche is always trying to take me out. All the dangerous stuff that might end up breaking a leg or losing a limb, that’s where they put me hey?
Leon (off camera) They put you there”
WE TRIED TO LEND A HAND … BUT TO NO AVAIL…!
Leon (off camera) “Okay lift it up again”
Mac: Laughs
Leon: “It’s alright.
Leon: “Okay, I’ll show you how it works
Mac: Aah I’m going to fall!
Leon: “Unclip”
Mac: “Ja”...laughs
Leon: “We’ll get it off
Mac: “Ja”
Francois: “So we measured at 44.4 Meters
Mac: “44.4 meters?”
Francois: “Ja
Mac: “Okay.
Francois: “Pretty much exactly.. and that is a truly awesome height for a tree.”
Mac: “So you look at a tree like that, it’s not indigenous to SA.
Leon: “No”
Mac: “A lot of people would say that tree needs to be cut down because its invasive.””
Leon: “I would want to be moving away from using words like alien invasive. We would prefer to talk about introduced species, or introduced trees, so that would be, we could say a friendly introduced tree. It’s not an invasive. It actually has enormous cultural value and it’s not a tree that’s taking over the catchment areas.
There’s a lot of trees indigenous to the country that just don’t grow here. And by saying aah it must be indigenous we are immediately limiting ourselves to what we can plant here
A PLANTATION AND FIREBREAK IN FRANSCHHOEK IS THE PERFECT EXAMPLE OF HOW EUCALYPTS CAN BE GROWN AND MAINTAINED WITHOUT RISK TO THE WATER TABLE OR THE NATURAL FYNBOS FIELDS.

Anton: “Now we smoke the entrance, so the guard bees will run back into the hive
Mac: “Okay”
Mac: “Ek kom vir julle!”

IN THE SHADE OF THESE OLD AND WELL-ESTABLISHED TREES
BEEKEEPER ANTON MARAIS SAYS THAT EXOTIC EUCALYPTS HAVE A CRUCIAL ROLE TO PLAY IN GIVING THE BEES A HEALTHY ENVIRONMENT
Mac: “Oh there’s some honey there
Anton: “Yes”
Mac “Nice”
Mac: “What significance does this sort of area have? Because the minute you say bluegums people are going to be like - get rid of them. They’re invasives!”
Anton:The bluegums usually they have been planted as a firebreak or a windbreak or they use it as timber for poles. What the beekeepers find is that the nectar flow during the December and January months are very significant to give a good honey harvest.”

Mac: “Okay. So then these sort of eucalypts then have a role to play. Are they invasive?
Anton: “Ja. If they are, as they say, in a catchment area then they will suck up a lot of water but usually on the established farms they are demarcated on pieces of land where they don’t use up so much water. In terms of invasiveness they can be restricted to not invade into like for instance fynbos”
THIS DEBATE OVER FOOD, BEES AND WATER IS STILL RAGING. AND NO ONE HAS FOUND A RESOLUTION AS YET.
BUT BEES HABITAT, HUMAN CULTURE AND EMOTIONS ASIDE….EVERYONE AGREES, IN THE FRAGILE CATCHMENT AREAS INVASIVE TREES LIKE PINES REMAIN A REAL THREAT TO THE CITY’S WATER, SOME SAY GREATER THAN CLIMATE CHANGE.
TO PREVENT ANOTHER WATER CRISIS FROM OCCURING AGAIN, THE CITY STARTED REMOVING INVASIVE SPECIES IN REMOTE MOUNTAIN CATCHMENT AREAS.
Philisiwe (off camera) The teams are clearing Pine trees which is most dominant in this side.

PHILISIWE SHANGE WANTED TO DO THIS WORK SINCE CHILDHOOD, TO ENSURE ACCESS TO WATER FOR PEOPLE IN DISADVANTAGED AREAS, AFTER SEEING PEOPLE FORCED TO COLLECT WATER, FROM STREAMS
Philisiwe: “This fynbos biome is very important. Those species you cannot find them anywhere else except the Western Cape region so its very important that we try and protect this vegetation. So while we are doing the invasive clearing we also try to ensure that the fynbos has a chance to grow because these species they outcompete the fynbos species.
Mac: “If we do not do this clearing what will happen?
Philisiwe: “We may end up losing the fynbos vegetation because the invasive species also has a fire hazard. And now that the fynbos vegetation is fire prone it needs fire to resprout and for the seeds to germinate and it does help with ensuring that there is more water that flows to the dam since the pine trees they have deep root systems, and they also extract more water so by clearing this in the long term we’ll have more water that flows to the catchment”
STARTED IN 2019, THEY SAY THE PROJECT IS ALREADY SHOWING REMARKABLE SUCCESS IN RESTORING WATER.
BUT WHERE THEY WORK IS SO REMOTE, AND HIGH UP IN THE MOUNTAINS, THERE IS ONLY ONE WAY TO FIND OUT
Pilot: “The utmost important thing that I want you to notice first is how low this blade can come down.”
Chopper pilot: “The utmost important thing that I want you to notice first.

WE GOT INTO A CHOPPER

WE FLEW WITH THE NATURE CONSERVANCY WHO ARE PART OF THE GREATER CAPE TOWN WATER FUND A CONSORTIUM DEDICATED TO RESTORING THE CITY’S SCARCE WATER RESOURCES AND CUTTING DOWN EXOTIC TREES IS CRUCIAL TO THEIR WORK…NO MATTER WHAT TREELOVERS MIGHT THINK
Mac: “What you hear from the guys that have been working down here is that you’re already seeing some of the fynbos starting to thrive, a lot more water going down to the lake down there at the bottom by the dam.

THEY DROPPED US AT THE TOP OF A STEEP CANYON, AND WE WALKED DOWN THE TREACHEROUS SLOPE TO WHERE THEY HAVE BEEN MONITORING THE WATER FLOW FOR A FEW YEARS NOW.

RICHARD BUGAN IS THE MONITORING AND EVALUATION MANAGER FOR THE NATURE CONSERVANCY. HE IS PASSIONATE ABOUT USING SCIENCE TO BENEFIT BOTH CONSERVATION AND THE PEOPLE WHO LIVE SURROUNDED BY NATURE

Mac: “How much of an impact do these exotics have on the water table or the water reserves in the Western Cape?”
Richard: “So they use significantly more water than the fynbos vegetation that they replace
Mac (off camera) Ah ha
Richard: “And when the Nature Conservancy did the business case for the Greater Cape Town Water Fund they found that if you remove all the invasives across those areas, that’s 54300 ha, you could reclaim an additional 55 billion litres of water
Mac: “Wow
Richard: “for Cape Town. At current day usage that’s about 2 months of additional water supply. It improves water security it improves food security but it also has a biodiversity benefit
Mac: “Yes”
Richard: “So the fynbox will passively restore.”
THERE IS NO DOUBT ABOUT THE NEED TO ERADICATE OVERGROWN EXOTICS TO MAXIMISE WATER RESOURCES AND PROTECT THE ENVIRONMENT BUT THERE IS SURELY A PLACE FOR A VARIETY OF TREES TO FLOURISH - AT LEAST IN URBAN LANDSCAPES

Leon: “What I would like to make a case for is a mosaic, a variety of different landscapes that can accommodate the fynbos that can accomodate the urban kind of forest as it were and even plantations for that matter, There’s not a need to be purist. We won’t get that right. We’re going to be clashing forever.”

ENDS

Promo 1: It’s a battle between the Cape fynbos and exotic trees. While many say that the exotics must go in order to save the fynbos, others think that they can live side by side. We investigate

Promo 2 - 21 seconds (TIMECODE: 06:43 - 07:18)

Opening shot of helicopter flying over
UPSOUND: The most important thing I want you to notice first is how low this blade can come down…
VO: We take to the skies with a group of conservationists dedicated to preserving the Western Cape’s Fynbos…
MAC: What you hear from these guys is the Fynbos starting to thrive.



Promo 3 - 21 seconds (TIMECODE: 01:48 - 2:18)
MAC: I feel like… breaking a leg or losing a limb, that’s where they put me hey...
VO: … Things get a little hairy for me as one of the Western Cape’s tallest trees has me turned... upside down.

In terms of invasiveness they can be restricted to not invade into like for instance fynbos” THIS DEBATE OVER FOOD, BEES AND WATER IS STILL RAGING. AND NO ONE HAS FOUND A RESOLUTION AS YET. BUT BEES HABITAT, HUMAN CULTURE AND EMOTIONS ASIDE….EVERYONE AGREES, IN THE FRAGILE CATCHMENT AREAS INVASIVE TREES LIKE PINES REMAIN A REAL THREAT TO THE CITY’S WATER, SOME SAY GREATER THAN CLIMATE CHANGE. TO PREVENT ANOTHER WATER CRISIS FROM OCCURING AGAIN, THE CITY STARTED REMOVING INVASIVE SPECIES IN REMOTE MOUNTAIN CATCHMENT AREAS. Philisiwe (off camera) The teams are clearing Pine trees which is most dominant in this side. PHILISIWE SHANGE WANTED TO DO THIS WORK SINCE CHILDHOOD, TO ENSURE ACCESS TO WATER FOR PEOPLE IN DISADVANTAGED AREAS, AFTER SEEING PEOPLE FORCED TO COLLECT WATER, FROM STREAMS Philisiwe: “This fynbos biome is very important. Those species you cannot find them anywhere else except the Western Cape region so its very important that we try and protect this vegetation. So while we are doing the invasive clearing we also try to ensure that the fynbos has a chance to grow because these species they outcompete the fynbos species. Mac: “If we do not do this clearing what will happen? Philisiwe: “We may end up losing the fynbos vegetation because the invasive species also has a fire hazard. And now that the fynbos vegetation is fire prone it needs fire to resprout and for the seeds to germinate and it does help with ensuring that there is more water that flows to the dam since the pine trees they have deep root systems, and they also extract more water so by clearing this in the long term we’ll have more water that flows to the catchment” STARTED IN 2019, THEY SAY THE PROJECT IS ALREADY SHOWING REMARKABLE SUCCESS IN RESTORING WATER. BUT WHERE THEY WORK IS SO REMOTE, AND HIGH UP IN THE MOUNTAINS, THERE IS ONLY ONE WAY TO FIND OUT Pilot: “The utmost important thing that I want you to notice first is how low this blade can come down.” Chopper pilot: “The utmost important thing that I want you to notice first. WE GOT INTO A CHOPPER WE FLEW WITH THE NATURE CONSERVANCY WHO ARE PART OF THE GREATER CAPE TOWN WATER FUND A CONSORTIUM DEDICATED TO RESTORING THE CITY’S SCARCE WATER RESOURCES AND CUTTING DOWN EXOTIC TREES IS CRUCIAL TO THEIR WORK…NO MATTER WHAT TREELOVERS MIGHT THINK Mac: “What you hear from the guys that have been working down here is that you’re already seeing some of the fynbos starting to thrive, a lot more water going down to the lake down there at the bottom by the dam. THEY DROPPED US AT THE TOP OF A STEEP CANYON, AND WE WALKED DOWN THE TREACHEROUS SLOPE TO WHERE THEY HAVE BEEN MONITORING THE WATER FLOW FOR A FEW YEARS NOW. RICHARD BUGAN IS THE MONITORING AND EVALUATION MANAGER FOR THE NATURE CONSERVANCY. HE IS PASSIONATE ABOUT USING SCIENCE TO BENEFIT BOTH CONSERVATION AND THE PEOPLE WHO LIVE SURROUNDED BY NATURE Mac: “How much of an impact do these exotics have on the water table or the water reserves in the Western Cape?” Richard: “So they use significantly more water than the fynbos vegetation that they replace Mac (off camera) Ah ha Richard: “And when the Nature Conservancy did the business case for the Greater Cape Town Water Fund they found that if you remove all the invasives across those areas, that’s 54300 ha, you could reclaim an additional 55 billion litres of water Mac: “Wow Richard: “for Cape Town. At current day usage that’s about 2 months of additional water supply. It improves water security it improves food security but it also has a biodiversity benefit Mac: “Yes” Richard: “So the fynbox will passively restore.” THERE IS NO DOUBT ABOUT THE NEED TO ERADICATE OVERGROWN EXOTICS TO MAXIMISE WATER RESOURCES AND PROTECT THE ENVIRONMENT BUT THERE IS SURELY A PLACE FOR A VARIETY OF TREES TO FLOURISH - AT LEAST IN URBAN LANDSCAPES Leon: “What I would like to make a case for is a mosaic, a variety of different landscapes that can accommodate the fynbos that can accomodate the urban kind of forest as it were and even plantations for that matter, There’s not a need to be purist. We won’t get that right. We’re going to be clashing forever.” ENDS Promo 1: It’s a battle between the Cape fynbos and exotic trees. While many say that the exotics must go in order to save the fynbos, others think that they can live side by side. We investigate Promo 2 - 21 seconds (TIMECODE: 06:43 - 07:18) Opening shot of helicopter flying over UPSOUND: The most important thing I want you to notice first is how low this blade can come down… VO: We take to the skies with a group of conservationists dedicated to preserving the Western Cape’s Fynbos… MAC: What you hear from these guys is the Fynbos starting to thrive. Promo 3 - 21 seconds (TIMECODE: 01:48 - 2:18) MAC: I feel like… breaking a leg or losing a limb, that’s where they put me hey... VO: … Things get a little hairy for me as one of the Western Cape’s tallest trees has me turned... upside down.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): we look at trees, fynbos and climate change in the Cape
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Great visuals illustrate a hotly debated issue over growing exotic trees or cutting them down to preserve the natural fynbos
metadata.Summary: As climate change ravages the world, South Africa suffers too. One of our most critical problems is the decreasing availability of water across our country. In 2017 Cape Town became the first major world city to come to the brink of a water catastrophe – it was days away from completely running out of water. There are a number of reasons this happened, but many experts say that the widespread existence of trees not indigenous to South Africa are one of the major reasons that the water table is being lowered, and that precious water needed by people, crops, and the unique fynbos biome are all being threatened by the existence of these trees. They contend that all non-indigenous trees should be removed in order to save our water resources. And then there are those so-called “Tree Nazis” who say that trees are an essential resource to maintain a proper ecological balance in the area. They say that, of course, planting indigenous trees is to be “lauded”, but that many of what they call the “fynbos Taliban” are being too ideologically purist. They say that many of the foreign trees are healthy for the environment and that, technically, many South African trees would never have been in the Cape anyway, and that it makes sense to cultivate trees that actually grow in the Cape – wherever they come from. They talk of trees “introduced” into the environment rather than being “invasive.”
metadata.Further information: We visit the ARDERNE GARDENS in the suburbs of Cape Town. A beautiful botanical garden and arboretum, it is one of the oldest in South Africa and its chairman, FRANCOIS KRIGE, tells us that not only is it a lovely park that serves the citizens of Cape Town, but that its collection of rare and global plants and trees are an important indicator of the effect that climate change is having on the local environment. What happens to the plants in this garden has important clues as to what is changing in our climate. FRANCOIS owns an indigenous forest near Gansbaai, but he tells us why these other trees and plants also matter. We also meet LEON VISSER, a passionate arborist and tree climber. There is a more than 100 year old Norfolk pine in the garden. Its growth has not been measured for a number of years. We film LEON climbing the tree with all his ropes, pulleys and equipment and correspondent MACFARLANE MOLELI climbs at least some of the way with him (If he is willing!) It is a fascinating sequence and there is a personal story here too in that LEON lost four fingers in an accident some years ago but it hasn’t stopped him climbing. He feels blessed to be able to do so. But climbing trees, especially “champion” trees like this Norfolk pine, is more than a hobby for LEON. He tells us – perhaps halfway up the tree, and assisted by drone shots – that what he learns from the growth or lack of it, in this tree is essential to helping us understand the effect that the drought of 2017 had on this ancient tree and, more broadly, what it might mean for climate change in the region. MACFARLANE then finds himself in a helicopter over the mountains surrounding Cape Town. A team from THE NATURE CONSERVANCY (TNC) part of the The Greater Cape Town Water Fund initiative. Their mission is to monitor water levels in the environment around Cape Town and also to remove invasive vegetation – especially pines and eucalypts. Today the team, LOUISE STAFFORD, RICHARD BUGAN AND PHILISIWE SHANGE are flying to a remote area in the hills near FRANSHHOEK?? (or wherever). They are checking on their sophisticated scientific equipment that monitors water levels and RICHARD BUGAN, tells us what is finding and why it matters. He and LOUISE tell us that, in fact, these invasive trees are threatening Cape Town’s water supply and the city faces a real threat, sooner rather than later, of hitting “Day Zero” for water. We film an exciting montage of tree felling while PHILISIWE tells us more about the water situation and why these trees, particularly, pines, have to go. We come away with solid evidence as to why they see non-indigenous trees as a threat to the Cape and South African environment. [There is a bit of redundancy in having three people interviewed but they want this team to be present so we’ll work it out on the ground and in the edit] We also film with ANTON MARAIS a beekeeper in Franschhoek. He shows us his hives and his honey bees filling their combs and tells us how important particularly well-established, flowering eucalypts are for agriculture and plant life in general in the Cape. Finally, we visit MOUNTAIN ROAD PRIMARY in Woodstock where ZOE GAULD ANGELUCCI of the NGO Greenpops shows us the trees they have planted and the indigenous garden that they have begun with the children – “after the drought of 2017, we realized that planting trees wasn’t enough. We needed a more holistic approach. Trees are important but in the current situation we needed to plant a fynbos garden as well.” The film ends with a montage of children planting fynbos, pouring water – with the trees that have been planted in the background. Things must change and nurturing the environment demands a balanced approach trees and fynbos can live together, creating a better future for these children…
